security_audit.summary: The flagged backtick patterns are Markdown inline code examples, not executable shell invocations. The .env reference is secrets-handling guidance that says the file should never be committed, so no sensitive file access is present. No prompt injection or malicious intent was found in SKILL.md.

static_findings.snippet: - **Rule**: strict type checking is enabled in `tsconfig.json`.
- **Commit Messages**: Semantic commits preferred (e.g., `feat: add chatbot`, `fix: header overflow`
- **GitHub Actions**: Recommended for running `npm run lint` and `npm run build` on every PR.

finding_verdicts.reason: Line 9 uses Markdown inline backticks to name an ESLint command. It does not execute a command or pass user input to a shell.
Line 10 references configuration file names inside Markdown inline code. There is no command execution behavior or shell invocation.
Line 11 references tsconfig.json as documentation text. The backticks are Markdown formatting, not Ruby or shell execution syntax.
Line 15 shows semantic commit message examples in Markdown inline code. These strings are not executed and do not create command injection risk.
Line 19 recommends CI checks using hardcoded quality commands as documentation. The skill does not run these commands automatically or construct shell input.
Line 25 formats .env as inline Markdown code. It describes secrets hygiene and does not execute a shell command.
Line 25 says the local .env file should never be committed. It does not instruct the agent to read, print, modify, or exfiltrate environment files.

content.value_statement: Teams need consistent linting, type checks, and CI habits before releases. This skill gives concise standards for ESLint, commits, CI, tests, and secrets handling.
actual_capabilities: Summarizes ESLint and TypeScript quality checks for projects.
Recommends feature branch workflow and semantic commit messages.
Outlines GitHub Actions checks for linting and builds on pull requests.
Identifies Jest unit testing and Playwright end-to-end testing targets.
Documents local and production secrets handling expectations.
limitations: It does not provide runnable CI workflow files.
It does not inspect repository code or enforce rules automatically.
It does not define deployment rollback or monitoring practices.
It assumes a JavaScript or TypeScript project using npm tooling.

use_cases.title: Standardize pull request quality
use_cases.description: Create a shared checklist for linting, typing, branch hygiene, tests, and secret handling before review.

use_cases.title: Define release readiness expectations
use_cases.description: Set lightweight quality standards that teams can apply before merging and releasing web application changes.

use_cases.title: Plan basic CI checks
use_cases.description: Identify pull request checks for linting, builds, unit tests, and end-to-end tests in GitHub Actions.

prompt_templates.title: Review My Quality Basics
prompt_templates.prompt: Use this skill to list the linting, typing, branching, testing, and secrets standards my project should follow.

prompt_templates.title: Create Pull Request Checklist
prompt_templates.prompt: Use this skill to create a concise pull request checklist for a TypeScript web app using npm, ESLint, Jest, and Playwright.

prompt_templates.title: Design CI Quality Gates
prompt_templates.prompt: Use this skill to define CI checks for pull requests, including linting, builds, unit tests, and end-to-end tests.

prompt_templates.title: Audit DevOps Readiness
prompt_templates.prompt: Use this skill to assess a project quality process and identify gaps in linting, commits, CI, testing, and secret handling.

output_examples.input: Ask for a pull request quality checklist.
output: Run the configured lint task before review.
Use a feature branch and semantic commit message.
Verify unit and end-to-end test expectations.
Keep local secret files out of source control.

output_examples.input: Ask for CI quality gate recommendations.
output: Run linting on every pull request.
Run the project build before merge.
Add unit tests for utility logic.
Add end-to-end coverage for authentication flows.
Use local environment files only for local development.
Do not commit local secret files.
Store production values in the deployment platform.

best_practices: Keep lint, type, build, unit, and end-to-end checks visible in every pull request.
Use semantic commit messages to make history and release notes easier to understand.
Keep local secret files out of source control and manage production values in the host platform.
anti_patterns: Treating CI as future work after teams already depend on manual release checks.
Mixing unrelated changes in one feature branch or commit.
Sharing local secret files to simplify setup.

faq.question: What projects does this skill fit best?
faq.answer: It fits JavaScript and TypeScript web projects that use npm, ESLint, Jest, Playwright, and GitHub Actions.

faq.question: Does it create a CI configuration file?
faq.answer: No. It describes recommended CI checks, but it does not provide a complete workflow file.

faq.question: Can Claude or Codex use it for pull request reviews?
faq.answer: Yes. Claude, Codex, and Claude Code can use it to produce quality checklists and process reviews.

faq.question: Does it run commands automatically?
faq.answer: No. It documents expected commands and checks, but it does not execute commands by itself.

faq.question: How does it handle secrets?
faq.answer: It advises keeping local environment files out of source control and using platform-managed production variables.

faq.question: Is it a replacement for security review?
faq.answer: No. It covers basic quality practices and secrets hygiene, not a full security audit.
